utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We apologise for the delay, noting it was March we were waiting inside courtroom I. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bulatovic. Yesterday we spoke -- at the end we spoke about the expulsion of people and I would like to address some occasions where you discussed it in the SDC meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 06244 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, Mr. Bulatovic, these are the shorthand notes of the 8th Session of the SDC of 12th March 1993. Can we please have page 31 in the English and page 25 in the B/C/S. Mr. Bulatovic, I would like to quote what you said on -- and you say here: "We are obliged to help them," referring to Republika Srpska, "but we are also obliged to understand that we can hardly co-operate with someone who, like the Prime Minister of the RS advises us to ethnically cleanse Sandzak and kill the Muslims there." And can we have the next page in the English. And then you also say: "The Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, Mr. Lukic, he advises us to do it as soon as possible, for Muslims are not to be trusted. They will stab us in the back, they will mine our railroad, and so on." Mr. Bulatovic, that's what you said and that was your information; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this meeting very well. It was being decided how to meet the requests of the Government of Republika Srpska for their military conscripts to be arrested, those who are in the territory of the FRY and how to deliver them by force to the VRS. That decision was not taken and I'm very proud about that. This passage deals with the decision-making process. It is true that this decision was not notified to us in person, but we were just told that in the ranks of the Government of Republika Srpska occasionally there are some extreme views. It turned out that those extreme views were something we could not share, they were not our convictions, and they could not support the making of the decision that was asked of us to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move on to page 46 in the English and page 37 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you say here that is one -- and you speak about the murder of Muslims committed by the Lukic group in this context. You say the following: "That is one of the most important elements of our national strategy, all the more so because the highest leadership of Republika Srpska suggests that we should initiate organised ethnic cleansing and that would be a disaster." That was your position at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't have that text in front of me. If it could be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. It should be page 37 and -- not page 37, it's page 37 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we are seeing on this page, upper part, the first big paragraph, last sentence of that paragraph. In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In English, but I can't see it now here in the B/C/S. Can we see the previous page. That should be -- sorry, that was a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You see here how you speak about -- it should be there: "That is one of the most important elements of our national strategy ..." It should be the second paragraph of where you are speaking. No, it's not. It can't be. Can we have the next -- the second-next page. Yes. Here you see it basically in where you speak. It's the third paragraph in which you speak, and that is -- that should be the quote that I had: "That is one of the most important elements of our national strategy, all the more so because the highest leadership of Republika Srpska suggests that we should initiate organised ethnic cleansing and that would be a disaster." That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But look, this was a normal and responsible reaction to an atrocious crime that was committed. This is a discussion about what the paramilitary unit of Mr. Lukic had done. They had killed innocent citizens of Serbia and Montenegro. They were killed on the train only because they were Muslims. You see in the text a strong conviction of that. There is talk about Lukic and he is described as a horrible person. The text also speaks about our efforts to preserve peace and tolerance. Sandzak, for your information, Your Honours, is an area populated mainly by Muslims. That's why I said one of the main elements of our state strategy was to preserve peace and tolerance. And the sentence that comes next is linked to the previous one where we describe an extremist excess by one person from the leadership --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure the translation of Mr. Bulatovic's answer has been translated. Yes, we'll hear what you say, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to draw your attention to the fact that Mr. Bulatovic said it was one of the most important elements of our state strategy, all the more so because from the highest -- it originates from the highest places in Republika Srpska, whereas the interpretation refers to the "highest leadership of Republika Srpska." He actually said from the highest places in Republika Srpska. "Highest places" is not legally the same as the "highest leadership."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic is kindly asked by interpreters to speak a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, for the benefit of the interpreters, could you kindly speak a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, when you -- I assume that "highest places" is the correct translation as Mr. Karadzic says, and "highest places" means the Bosnian Serb leadership or who would you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear. This is a continuation from the same session where we strenuously condemn the then-Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this document please be admitted, Your Honour? And I assume we do it like with the Defence exhibits, to assume it -- to admit it in full. We do have -- in fact, throughout this session we have references to where they speak about the Republika Srpska and the relationships between the two entities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we need entire transcript which takes place in -- outside Republika Srpska? Yes, I will hear from the Defence. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We join in the Prosecution's request because these are snippets of the discussion. It's possible we could compact it more if that was preferable to the Chamber and take only those portions relating to Bosnia and excerpt those. But in principle the discussion continues for more than the pages that are referenced here and it would be useful, I think, for the Chamber to have the full discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you are not minded to do this, I just wanted to mention that the following pages are about discussions, and that is in addition to those that I just mentioned. It would be 31, 32, 45 to 47, that's where the topic basically comes up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm fine with admitting those pages, but why do we have to admit even the irrelevant parts? Are we happy to admit those pages referred to by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In principle, Mr. President, but we'd also like to take a look at it to see if there's other portions of the transcript where this topic is discussed. So if you would allow us to do that, we could come back to you with the pages that we would agree could be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you could live with this suggestion by Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll admit those pages referred to by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Shall we give the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we now please have 65 ter 07528.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, Mr. Bulatovic, we have again shorthand notes of a session of the SDC, and it's the 14th Session from 11 October 1993. You may remember that there was a session that -- where General Perisic proposed a new scheme of payment of VJ officers serving in the VRS and the SRK. And can we please move to page 26 in both languages and it's the first paragraph in both. And you say here,

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: "Let's be completely frank in our close circles. We are facing or shall very soon face the fact that a degree of ideologisation is present in quite an extent both in Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina and their respective armies, but it would be difficult to introduce here that Chetnik ideology present over there." You said that, Mr. Bulatovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Should it be indicated for the sake of interpreters what part of the text is cited.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph, should be the first paragraph in both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In English it starts from the last part of the third sentence -- the third line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I'd ask you whether you said that and you haven't -- not yet answered that. You said that; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. I said that. I'm familiar with all these transcripts from the Supreme Defence Council. I believe they are accurate and they faithfully reflect everything that was said there. This was a discussion about how the Army of Yugoslavia was coming into being because the Yugoslav People's Army before that, if you will let me explain why I said this --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have your permission to explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would rather move on to the next page and perhaps it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, let's continue. If Mr. Karadzic wishes to take up that issue he will later on. Let's continue for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move to page 28 in the English and it's also page 28 in the B/C/S, and it's again the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the same topic you say here: "If someone has spent a long time in Bosnia, it's hard to appoint him to a position in Novi Sad now. We have to bear in mind that people change in war in an atmosphere and in the logic of war and this is a political option which we don't quite accept here but we support it because it's in our interest." Mr. Bulatovic, Novi Sad is a multi-ethnic town with a lot of non-Serb population in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true about Novi Sad, but at issue here is Novi Pazar, and Novi Pazar has a 70 per cent Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It says here in your -- at least in the English it says "Novi Sad." Is that a mistake or -- when you look at the B/C/S it says "Novi Sad."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's obviously a mistake. You don't have to know the language. Look at the passage in B/C/S. In the original it says "Novi Pazar"; in the translation it says "Novi Sad."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You're right. You're right. I now see it. I was looking for that word. Thank you. You said already it's a multi -- it's a Muslim-populated area and those who spent long time in the Republika Srpska would not want to live among non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the conclusion is completely different. This discussion is about officers, people with combat experience, people who had waged war and who, in my view - as you can see from this document - cannot now be transferred to be commanders in peace time in other environments. Because it says here "war changes people." This is saying that we need to take account of the realities and preserve peace in Serbia and in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can these documents be admitted, and I also mention here that the pages that are concerned with Republika Srpska are pages 24 to 30. That's at least how I saw it, but maybe Mr. Robinson will want to make the same comment as previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no objection. We'll let you know -- or we'll let the Prosecution know also if we have some additional pages we think should be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the page number that we saw now?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The page number that I was actually discussing with Mr. Bulatovic was 26 and 28, but the entire is 24 to 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them, pages from 24 to 30.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the incorrect bits of the translation are prejudicial to the Defence, I would like to have the accuracy of the translation checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is being done on an ongoing basis. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 06260 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bulatovic, as again shorthand notes from the SDC and it's the 2nd of November, 1994, and it's the 28th Session. And just so -- to remind you, in this session the rejection of the peace plan by the Bosnian Serbs were -- was discussed, and General Perisic gave a briefing on the military situation in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move to page 7 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's look at -- Mr. Perisic is speaking and it's the paragraph, the upper paragraph in the B/C/S and the first paragraph also -- the second paragraph in the English. And he says here: "Out of a total number of population of the entire area, 20 per cent Serbs hold more than 70 per cent of the territory, which is unsustainable." Mr. -- that's -- Mr. Bulatovic, you were aware that the Bosnian Serb claimed a large percentage of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was a matter of constant debate in the SDC; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is true that we have a document before us which is authentic and reflects faithfully the words of General Perisic. What follows from this is not a political acknowledgement of how much territory Serbs should hold. It was not we who discussed that; it was the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia. There were negotiations about this and similar views that resulted in the Dayton Accords. It's true General Perisic said this, but this was said in the context of our efforts to bridge our differences with the leadership of Republika Srpska and to receive a political mandate for the decisions that ultimately resulted in the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move on to page 45 in the English and it is page 40 in the B/C/S, and in the B/C/S it's at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And here we have again General Perisic and he's saying -- in the B/C/S it's at the bottom. He's saying: "Time in running out and what transpired now is pure one-party army of the SDS. We can also pronounce the aforementioned army as Chetnik army or the one that give us hell in the near future. We should bear that in mind." Mr. Bulatovic, that is how it was seen by Perisic at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the point? How can President Bulatovic respond to Perisic's communist views?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no, I think that's an intervention that is not appropriate. That's a matter that he should raise later in his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the question as formulated is that you are asking Mr. Perisic's view to Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I simply asked him whether that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- Perisic's view and expressed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit, Your Honours, that it's very difficult for me to follow the sense. I have confirmed the truthfulness of these documents. It is indisputable on that basis that this is what General Perisic said at that point in time, but I think it's illusory to ask what Momir Bulatovic thinks about that when you have right below that what Momir Bulatovic thinks in that same period. And then as the document goes on when we're to read it in its entirety you could see that this opinion of General Perisic did not win out and it was not the operative opinion. It's very simple to read on and to see what Momir Bulatovic thought and what Slobodan Milosevic said and what was the conclusion of that state body in response to the views of Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest to admit the entire document because it's really only about the situation about Republika Srpska, their stances, and the stances that the participants of the SDC have on this topic. But of course I didn't much time to go into much more details, so that's my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So whole of 70 pages is related to matters in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so, although the gist of this discussion is from page 1 to 46, but it's nevertheless always coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given the circumstances the Chamber will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to discuss one more bit from the transcript of the "Death of Yugoslavia" interview, and can we please have P3060 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, did you sort out the question why it was noted as sometime in October 1994?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I must admit, I haven't. But I -- I think actually it is correct because when we look at other interviews that were given at that time, I know them from other cases, they are actually in 1994. That's what I think. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But witness testified it was around 2000, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, he did but I think he's mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But we will look into this and inform everyone. But here is the wrong exhibit. I obviously have made a mistake. Can we have 65 ter 24585, so obviously got the P number wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And can we move to page 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bulatovic, you speak here of a trip to Pale and you already -- we already discussed it. And you say here: "But it was an interesting and difficult journey because we saw for ourselves what war means. When you saw a signpost on the territory under Serbian control you knew that if the village was destroyed it must have been a Muslim village. Everything was empty and destroyed. A hundred or two hundred metres after that you have a village where everything is normal, children go to school, and you can't even imagine that this is a war zone." And you also speak about Pale being a real city and that there was no sign that a war was raging all around. And you say: "That's when I realised how terrible war is because there were ethnically pure Serb, Muslim, and Croat villages and this insanity must stop." Mr. Bulatovic, that's how you experienced the trip; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I experienced the entire war in Bosnia, which was tragic, it was equally unfair or unjust towards all, and it should have been stopped as soon as possible. This road was going through Serb territory and it was logical for us to pass through that way. In other areas, unfortunately, it was the other way around, where Serb villages were destroyed, where the Muslims and the Croats were predominantly living. This was just tragic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this document -- these pages 25 and 26 be admitted. That's the context of the travelling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be added to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have now the - I also don't have the D number - 65 ter 06141 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bulatovic, you have read this Council for Co-ordination of State Policy notes of the 18th August 1992 meeting and you discussed it with the Defence. And I only want to go to page 19 in the B/C/S and page 18 in the English. And we have Mr. Milan Panic, the then-Prime Minister, say here the following: "This afternoon I received the following information: Ethnic cleansing has begun. 15.000 Muslims from Sanski Most were given eight hours to leave their homes and make 20 kilometres to Jajce in order to reach the Muslims. This information was received from the United Nations." Mr. Bulatovic, this information that Mr. Panic is here providing was true, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that is accurate according to me is the following -- well, we don't know if this information is correct or not, but what is the reaction is that if it is so, that must be prevented. And that, in my opinion, is the only truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just to -- in the next page -- we need the next page in the English but the B/C/S is the same. And you -- and Mr. Panic says: "It's important that we discuss here whether it's possible to stop the war and to take an attitude that we don't provide assistance to ethnic cleansing and financing the war of the Serbs in Bosnia." And can we now go to page 75 in the English and 92 in the B/C/S. And Milan Panic asked General Zivota Panic what could be done and how to stop the artillery fire on Sarajevo, the battle in Bihac, the battle in Gorazde? Mr. Panic even says: "We could be better help to them if we would take their weapons from them." And General Panic says: "We cannot take their weapons away because that would be the war between us and them." That was a dilemma that the leadership in Yugoslavia -- Serbia and Montenegro you yourself were in; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been placed in an illogical position again to interpret what the dilemma is between Milan Panic and Zivota Panic. The transcripts are accurate, the words are accurate, but I would kindly ask Madam Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber to act as in the previous case. This document can be valid but in its entirety. It is very uncomfortable if you're asking me about certain sentences according to some Richelieu model. I think the entirety of the document is all right, but I cannot comment authoritatively on certain sections of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move on. Page 75 in the English at the bottom, I think it's there, and then we have page 93 in the B/C/S and it's also at the bottom. And Mr. Zivota Panic, or General Zivota Panic, states that the Bosnian Muslims planned the attack and they will move forward towards Jajce. They launched a heavy attack against Bihac. And then he refers to information that the Serbs when they came across a Muslim village they killed everybody from children to the elderly. Mr. Bulatovic, doing this, that's ethnic cleansing in its worst form, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I cannot see the text that you have just read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's page 93 in the B/C/S at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah, it's actually the last bit here, the last bit of Zivota Panic where he speaks about "Muslimansko selo ...," so --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask, this is a witness that is too important and too prominent a figure for sentences to be truncated. Can the entire statement by Zivota Panic be read out, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a matter for the cross-examination -- for the re-direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the sentence itself that -- which may not be correct that the witness should have chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't think it's a matter of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But now he can read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is your question, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually wanted him just to confirm that this was said and that this is -- I asked him, actually, this is ethnic cleansing in its worst form, killing all inhabitants of a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it had taken place; is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, actually. Only whether when it took place that's ethnic cleansing in its worst form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, and I know Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is very fair, maybe she doesn't see this portion in the text, but it says: "We obtained some information, which may not be correct ..." And so I think what everyone's point is here is that you can't put something to a witness as if it's a fact when even the speaker said "it may not be correct." And then you also omitted the last sentence which said "they have no control over these forces" which is also an important element. So our point is if you are going to refer to text, you should not be so selective so it distorts the meaning to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My point is that now Mr. Bulatovic has the opportunity to read the entire paragraph so he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, can you -- can you -- that information that Zivota Panic is referring to, was that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to read what Zivota Panic said in this same place before that, just a little bit before on the same page. When Karadzic was talking the other day you heard that he had no control over the individuals who did this but you knew they did it. They launched a grenade on Sarajevo and it seemed as if they launched a thousand grenades. Some of them got drunk, they say, "Let's say launch one. I mean it's very damaging to all of us." Secondly, as to whether this information is accurate or not, we don't know. It's possible here that we have paramilitary formations here against whom we fought quite strictly. This is the greatest crime and savagery which was not motived by any political goals but by looting, theft, and the satisfaction of the lowest impulses. These were not regular units under anyone's control. These were bands or gangs of criminals that we tried to stop in every possible way, but as President Karadzic himself said at the time, you could not have had control over all of these individuals. These, as far as I'm concerned, are the worst war crimes against civilians, but I would not agree that it was part of any systematic plan of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, how much more would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would -- I still have three topics. One is the objective of the Bosnian Serbs and it is only one document, then I will address very briefly the paramilitary formations and it's also one document, and if time allows then I would also address one topic in relation to Foca. I would think it's something like 20 minutes if you would allow me that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please conclude by ten past 10.00. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Bulatovic, you mention in paragraph 10 of your statement that you -- to the fact that the peace proposals included some kind of division of Bosnia and allowed the Bosnian Serbs to have a certain level of autonomy, but the Bosnian Serbs as well as the leaders in Croatia -- the Serb leaders in Croatia and in Serbia and Montenegro wanted to live in one state. That was the end goal, so to speak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the starting position in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We all lived in one state so that one group of political thought and political representatives of the people wanted to keep the existing situation, to stay in the existing state, while another group wanted to break-up this state and create independent states. So that's when Pandora's Box flew open. The initial position of representatives, political representatives, of the Serbian people wherever they were in the territory of the former Yugoslavia was the survival of the state. It was status quo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have document 65 ter 06145 on the screen and it is a session of the Council for Co-Ordination of State Policy held on 9 January 1993, so that means we are now in 1993 and can we have both -- page 8 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have Mr. Krajisnik basically speaking here and summarising the position of the Bosnian Serbs that there is a prevailing opinion that it is crucial -- is a crucial comment when integration of all territories that want to form an undivided country is possible. I think of territory of Serbia, Montenegro, Serbian Krajina, and Republika Srpska." And that's in 1993. So it continued, this wish to unite the Serbian territories in three republics; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that is not right. This was the initial position here --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that all of these territories are in one --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I was just reading what Mr. Krajisnik was saying on the -- in 1993 on that session and he said that, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are discussing a document here which is called the harmonisation of the state policy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You -- I have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Harmonisation makes sense --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you because we have very little time, as you have heard. The answer is either yes or no, he said that. But the transcript is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, this has no probative value for him to simply say what is being in the transcript. He has to be given the opportunity to give his comment on it, otherwise there's no point in simply showing him something and asking him if the words appear on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know how to avoid being interrupted in any way. It's correct. The document exists and it's authentic what is stated here. But this is a document where different opinions are being harmonised, where on the basis of individual opinion, conclusions are drawn for political and state action. Individual opinions here do not have to win out or become a guide-line for the future action of state organs, either those in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or those in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this transcript be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the status of this document? I think we discussed this in -- during the course of Jovanovic testimony. Yes, Mr. Tieger, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe that particular quote was used. If -- I don't want to enter the fray about the extent of the admission of documents, but these -- the co-ordination council sessions were the subject of discussion between Mr. Robinson and myself about whether or not those were so closely related to the kinds of documents we admitted in their entirety that they should be as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question was it was not formally admitted before?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I checked that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It was discussed. Yes, what pages are you tendering, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My proposal would actually be to admit the entire document, otherwise I just referred to one particular page, now I can't find which it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is a document of 167 pages. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, in principle we favour the admission of the entire document or at least all those portions that relate to the discussion and Bosnia, and if that's too burdensome to you then the Prosecution can identify the pages that they believe are relevant and we would keep the option of adding to that if we think there are other parts that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you think identify the pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we could do that by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. On that basis, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P6164.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. -- the next topic I only very briefly want to discuss is volunteers and paramilitaries. And can we please have 65 ter 06242 on the screen, and it's the SDC minutes of 7th August 1992 and it's 5th Session of this. And you may recall that in this session you referred to problems of convoys of armed men constantly bussing through Pljevlja in Montenegro and how you wanted to stop it. I think you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. That was a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I just want to refer to page 4 in the English and it's also page 4 in the B/C/S and you describe the problem arising, and in paragraph 5 on this page you say that: "The fate and the existence of Muslims could have ended that night." You don't need to go into all these details, but these armed men were a threat to the Muslim population in Montenegro and it would be also to the Muslim population in Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a criminal paramilitary group that came from Cajnice, the territory of the Republika Srpska, and it was also assisted by the local population and they practically captured the town. They were more numerous and stronger than police and regular military forces and their political goal was to kill all Muslims. The Muslims made up 10 per cent of the Pljevlja local population at the time. I physically came and prevented this, and later we arrested these people. The problem with paramilitary formations, if you permit me, is the fact that you cannot stop them. Imagine a bus of armed people is supposed to be stopped by one policeman on the road. You need to have five times more armed people to stop something like that. The problem of the paramilitary forces was our biggest problem. It was also something that could be -- we could be blamed for the most and we were unable to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move to page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S and it is in the middle of the -- both pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you speak here about a self-proclaimed colonel who once was an active-duty officer, and you say the following: "Let's be honest, we needed those paramilitary formations for a while. They are now a great burden and a problem. People now changed sides based on these previous activities. It is now a sort of Seselj's army, his ranks." Mr. Bulatovic, does this refer to the Yellow Wasps, or to which particular group is that referring?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only has to do with one particular man, a madman, that's how I perceive him, a self-proclaimed colonel. And he considered himself to be one of Seselj's men. Seselj did not accept him at all. This was a time of madmen that you could not put into any kind of legal framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be admitted and I don't request now entire document, but the discussion of the paramilitaries and the effect they had in Montenegro, in particular, and Bosnia. That's on pages 1 to 29. The rest is unrelated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P6165.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now asking a few questions related to Foca and can we briefly into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, yesterday you mentioned that you were actually on -- you would speak to all sides in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and you also mentioned that you had good relations with Mr. Izetbegovic. And I wanted to ask you about one thing and that's -- relates to the beginning of the war, or rather, before, shortly before. Mr. Izetbegovic asked you to take over prisoners from the KP Dom in Foca who could not be kept safe in the territory, that he was worried about. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those prisoners were Muslims, right, and they were transferred?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were prisoners who were serving their sentences at the KP Dom, most of them were Muslim, because the majority population there is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned also yesterday that people from Bosnia-Herzegovina fled from that territory into Montenegro, and among them were also Muslims from Foca, Visegrad, Srebrenica, and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we're talking about two separate cases. President Izetbegovic in this case asked me -- do allow me. Do allow me --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please continue, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time there was still a single state there, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was all the same whether someone served their prison sentence on the basis of a judgement in Foca or in Danilovgrad. President Izetbegovic said that he was afraid that paramilitary formations headed by Arkan - those are his words - would go there and kill these people and he could not guarantee their security. And I said: Let them come to us. They came buses. They served their sentence at the prison in Spuz. The people served their sentences, and at the same time they saved themselves. This is a humanitarian gesture, and I thought it was my duty and obligation and I'm proud of having done this. There were also lots of refugees. A vast number of people were coming in. Some people disagreed with the policy of Radovan Karadzic. A lot of people didn't want to serve in the Army of Republika Srpska. A lot of people thought that their wives and children should come to the territory of Montenegro, and they came there and they had the status of refugees. My Montenegro then treated all of these people equally, as their own citizens. All children were enrolled in schools, regardless of whether they were Muslim or Serb, and people continued to receive their retirement pensions. There is unequivocal data about this from the UNHCR and also Mrs. Sadako Ogata thanked Montenegro and me personally several times for all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that, Mr. Bulatovic. But you also know that some of these Muslims from the territory, from Eastern Bosnia, were arrested in May 1992 by Montenegrin police and they were turned over the Serb police -- Bosnian Serb police and ended up in the KP Dom some of them did. Such cross-border activity was not done clandestinely on the local level; it involved higher levels, did it not? And my question would actually be: Were you involved in this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you mention a tragic incident. Recently it came to its judicial epilogue in the court system of the Republic of Montenegro and we heard that the Office of the Prosecutor of Montenegro contacted you, the Prosecutor's office here in The Hague, asking for your opinion. And what was said was that this was a case that had to be discussed within the judiciary of Montenegro. Recently an official judgement of acquittal was pronounced in relation to that indictment. No one is denying that these people suffered a tragic fate. At one point in time, they were repatriated to Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, none of the official organs from Montenegro could be held officially responsible for that. There is moral responsibility but the perpetrator should be sought elsewhere. After May 1992 when we officially recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina and when we withdrew all our units from Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the 27th of May there was not a single case of repatriation or, that is to say, returning persons who were refugees or who had fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, I take it you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please call up 65 ter 6145. Perhaps it already has a P number by now. It was displayed a moment ago. That is what Mr. Krajisnik said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, P6164.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to have page 7 in both English and in Serbian and then we're going to move on to page 8 probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see here that Mr. Krajisnik started to speak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now have the next page in both versions, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to draw your attention and the attention of all the other participants to the second paragraph. The speaker of the Assembly, Krajisnik, is presenting our view vis-a-vis the formation and survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that and I'm reading the paragraph now, and it clearly reflects Mr. Krajisnik's view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you to focus on the next paragraph -- no, not the next one, just skip one. And then look at the paragraph that the learned Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff quoted to you. And can you tell us whose opinion is being presented here by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is talking about the opinion of the Assembly, if I understand things correctly; because on the previous page he said that after the initial proposal of territorial delineation, or rather, reorganisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was discussed at the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. What would you take as his position and what would you -- and how would you characterise this, where it says there was a prevailing opinion or the opinion prevailed that, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to ask you to put an additional question to me. What is the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the second paragraph on this page, the one up there. Whose position is he presenting there and whose position is he presenting this other paragraph that starts with the words "the opinion prevailed that ..." and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly there were always groups that were called realists and groups that were called idealists. Some thought that this was a favourable moment whereas others thought that this could be achieved in another way and through different means. What is undeniable, I believe, is the wish to continue living within the common state or at least to have special ties between and among all these territories. However, this is a question of politics, who prevails when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you mentioned that it should be established whether an opinion prevailed and was reflected in decisions. Is it your position that it would be important to see the decisions, not only the discussion?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I shall withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was put to you today that you or somebody else in Yugoslavia as well advocated Serb plans about autonomy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you take part in meetings of leaderships of the Yugoslav republics with Lord Carrington early in June 1991 or throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I was president of Montenegro, I spent most of my term involved in peace negotiations about the reorganisation of Yugoslavia and the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I did a precise calculation. During my four-year term of office as president of Montenegro, I spent 110 days travelling and attending peace conferences and mostly discussing Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about your first term?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what the position was of the conference and particularly of President Izetbegovic with regard to these requests of ours, these demands of ours, maximum ones, to remain within Yugoslavia or, on the other hand, to have some autonomy in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crisis Staff in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia started when the then-ruling party, the League of Communists, disintegrated, and in the then-Federation that was the only party that existed. There was a long period of political torment and agony. The political organs did not really have the capacity to resolve any one of the issues involved. Because the organs were incapable of doing that, it was agreed upon that we, the six presidents of the Yugoslav republics, would find a political solution regarding the situation and the fate of the country. We did this under a great deal of public pressure and the media expected us to find a solution that would avoid war. The idea of the war was quite present in the media of our country even before the war started. Yugoslavia comes into existence and disappears as a result of major upheavals. It is the result of the First World War, and it was one of the first victims of the fascist aggression during the Second World War, and instinctively people were afraid what would happen when Yugoslavia would fall apart. The six of us, the Yugoslav presidents, travelled and the public called our meetings the travelling circus. As members of this circus, we were under constant pressure of media questions, whether there would be a war. What I particularly remember is that meeting, that was the last one in a series, that we had in Stojcevac near Sarajevo, and where finally we had been asked by the Yugoslav public to tell them whether there would be war, or rather, whether there would be an agreement. At this meeting Slovenia declared its decision to leave the Federation. Croatia personified by President Tudjman said that it would leave the Federation because it could not stay in it if Slovenia was not there. The most tragic person of that meeting was Alija Izetbegovic. There are stenograms that show this. And he said that if there's going to be a disintegration of Yugoslavia, a civil war would flare up in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said, I still remember his words: Armed groups are already gathering in hills. They're stopping people. There's no control over them. A war will break out. And then he asked that this compromise solution be accepted, the one that was submitted by him and the president of Macedonia, Kiro Gligorov. This proposal was not accepted. I remember that particularly because all the participants in the meeting were aware that in this situation when there was no political solution there has to be a war conflict. It wasn't that President Izetbegovic was accusing you, Mr. Karadzic, or any other political personality. He was just desperately struggling for a political solution that would not lead to chaos and chaos did happen when there was no political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In paragraph 7 of your statement you mention that meeting so I would like us to see 1D7816 in e-court. 1D7816. First of all, let us take a look at the first page. Are these the stenographic notes of that conference? No.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Again it's a meeting of the peace conference but it's not in June. It's in November -- no, October 1991. Can we now please take a look at page 25 and then 26?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to know how it arises from the cross-examination because I didn't speak about such early times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think thinking about the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, during the cross-examination the Prosecution did put a question related to the support of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, and President Bulatovic himself towards the demands of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina for autonomy. And perhaps he was being challenged in that way, or reprimanded, if you will, but now I would like to show what the situation was in the case of others. Was this a demand of Yugoslavia or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, and I don't think Mr. Bulatovic was ever reprimanded at all, but you are putting the question without knowing the document yourself. Why don't you put your question first and then, if necessary, you can put the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the position was vis-a-vis our demand? If we were not to stay in Yugoslavia, that we should within Bosnia-Herzegovina have our autonomy? What was the position of Lord Carrington? What was the position, say, of President Izetbegovic himself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then-European Community was actively involved in the entire process of the disintegration of Yugoslavia. The then so-called troika, headed by Mr. Hans van den Broek, came to Yugoslavia, and they asked Slovenia to postpone their departure from the common state. And they also asked Croatia to postpone the exercise of their state independence precisely in order to reach a solution for Bosnia. And the position of the conference on the former Yugoslavia was a result of that and it was supported by the leading powers of the world that were in the Contact Group, and that included the United States of America. Lord Carrington, in June 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: October 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- presented a plan and the plan was that those republics who wished to have independent states can do that. Point two was the republics that wish to remain together can do so. Point three said that there was special rights to be enjoyed by the Serb people in Croatia. And point four was resolving the question of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a special peace conference. For a simple reason, all of those who are involved in diplomacy and who sincerely wished to preserve peace know that Bosnia will behave just like Yugoslavia because Bosnia is a mini Yugoslavia. European diplomats envisaged a separate conference on Bosnia and this is shown by the fact that in this document that was shown to me, the words of Mr. Izetbegovic are recorded. Mr. Izetbegovic says himself in this text that he does not have the capacity to speak on behalf of all three ethnic communities. According to the then-constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a state, an equitable community of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Mr. Izetbegovic held the position of the president of the Presidency and this was based on the key aimed at equal representation. And he said that he had to check all of this with the representatives of the Serbs and Croats because as he himself said he did not have the capacity to pass a decision on behalf of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it surely goes beyond the scope of cross-examination. What Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff discussed with the witness is what was happening in Republika Srpska rather than the issue whether or not to support from the part of FRY or whatever. We'll have a break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could finish within ten minutes if it's easier so that we can let President Bulatovic go. Perhaps even less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for half an hour now and then take that opportunity to prepare yourself for more focused questions. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You already changed your seat, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And before Mr. Karadzic continues, I want to answer your question that you had in relation to the transcript for the "Death of Yugoslavia" interviews. We ourselves received this transcript on the 1st of November, 1995, and we believe that, indeed, the dates on this paper is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So would you like another opportunity to put that to Mr. Bulatovic? Having heard Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's comment, would you like to add anything with respect to the date of your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was put to me does not have a cover page or the indication of the author or anyone else. I do not contest the contents, but I remember that the BBC was making the "Death of Yugoslavia" series and did an interview with me in the office of my friend in Podgorica, that was the only office where I could talk, and I was no longer in power so I thought it was after 2000. But I don't think it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave it at that. Yes, Mr. Harvey, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to get to my feet earlier today, but may I please just take this opportunity to introduce Nemanja Ljubisavljevic, who has been manning our Belgrade office for some time and has been doing terrific work on an analysis of the B/C/S documents in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I was also going to note that the release date of the film of "Death of Yugoslavia" was, in fact, the 3rd of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, today on page 2 - in fact, it starts on page 1 and straddles page 2 - a quotation was given to you from what you said on the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on 12th March 1993. I'll read it now in English so it can be interpreted accurately: [In English] "Mr. Bulatovic, I would like to quote that you said -- what you said on -- and you say here: "'We are obliged to help them,' referring to the Republika Srpska, 'but we are also obliged to understand that we can hardly co-operate with someone who like the Prime Minister of the RS advises us to ethnically cleanse Sandzak and kill the Muslims there.'" [Interpretation] And in your answer -- in fact, the question also quotes: [In English] "The prime minister of Republika Srpska, Mr. Lukic, he advises us to do it as soon as possible, for Muslims are not to be trusted. They will stab us in the back. They will mine our railroad and so on." [Interpretation] In the second part of your answer you said this: [In English] "Pasic deals with the decision-making process. It is true that this decision was not notified to us in person, but we just -- we were just told that in the ranks of the Government of Republika Srpska occasionally there are some extreme views. It turned out that those extreme views were not something we could share. They were not our convictions and they could not support the making of the decision that was asked of us to make." [Interpretation] I should like to show you a document. Could we please call up 1D7303. Unfortunately, the translation is not ready yet, but you will be able to see for yourself what it is. It is the inaugural speech of Prime Minister Lukic before this session of the Supreme Defence Council, 19 January 1993. Could we look at page 5, I think. Yes. I will now read slowly what I want to put to you: "No matter how our enemies madly insist on continuing the war, we have to insist on the undertakings that this Assembly assumed by adopting the declaration to establish peace." And then further below it says: "As of today we have to start creating conditions for the citizens who had left their homes due to war operations, the feeling of personal insecurity and danger to their property, return to the territory of Republika Srpska when permanent peace is established. We have to guarantee to the citizens of other ethnicities all their rights according to the constitution and the laws. We made those undertakings and we have to meet them." And now I should like to take a look at the document that follows your session of the Supreme Defence Council, and that would be 1D7304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this is a correct way, a proper way of conducting your examination-in-chief or your re-examination. Why don't you put your question first instead of putting the document first? This is a typical way of leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'll take the blame for that because I advised Dr. Karadzic to do it this way and to ask the witness in light of what Prime Minister Lukic said how that tallies with what he had discussed in that meeting that was brought up by the Prosecution. So I don't think that that is leading, to put something in a neutral way to a witness and ask him how that tallies with the information that he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Lukic's statement in the Supreme Defence Council was put to the witness by the Prosecution, then he could have asked -- the accused could have asked whether the witness knew Mr. Lukic's position as a whole in general. And then he could put this document. Putting this document first is way of feeding some information to the witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you're entitled to do that so long as you ask the witness to comment on that in any way that he feels appropriate, so you're not leading the witness by presenting him with information and asking him for his views on it. It's a little more focused this way than to ask such a broad question and hope for a general answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I mean, this is a -- we've gone over this ground repeatedly, so I only rose to say this is actually a replication of an exchange we had not too long ago when I rose to say essentially that the formulation -- the last -- the formulation of the question doesn't neutralise the information previously provided to the witness. I referred to something that Judge Morrison had previously said basically to that effect, and there was agreement by the Court that that's the case. So I'm only standing to avoid an erosion of the standards that have been established over a long period of time and consistently maintained about the need to avoid leading questions. So I don't think that was a precisely fair, or at least precisely accurate, recollection by Mr. Robinson of the positions taken by the Trial Chamber on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, as you suggested, if Mr. Karadzic is to put -- to be putting something in a neutral way to the witness and ask how that would tally with the information that a witness has, but in the -- and given the past practice he's very much prone to ask leading questions. So that was the point that I made when I told him to put general question first, but we'll see how it evolves. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of what His Excellency Judge Kwon said on page 40, lines 20 and 21, about Lukic's statement at the Supreme Defence Council, can you explain, was Lukic present and did he state that at the Supreme Defence Council session?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the whole context it is obvious that the position of Mr. Lukic was conveyed to us in a hearsay way. We were just referring to a common place that was indirectly passed on to us in the absence of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your work, did you encounter similar positions of Mr. Lukic reflected in some reliable documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those positions were never officially stated, but the thinking of the Supreme Defence Council was that we did not want to co-operate with Republika Srpska based on extreme views. But since we were co-operating non-stop, in my view it is proof that their views were acceptable to both us and the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, how does what we saw in the previous document fit in with what reached you in that hearsay form?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is obvious. An official address by Prime Minister Lukic is something that cannot be objected to, whereas the information we received at the Supreme Defence Council was cause for great concern and for that reason was rejected by us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 6 of this document -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I just put this to you. This is the 7th Session of the cabinet after that meeting of yours, so on the 19th of May. We have one document from before the session and this one is after the session. I will read carefully the conclusions of the government. First sentence: "The report on the work of the commission for refugees and humanitarian aid for the first quarter of 1993 has been endorsed." And then further below it says: "Of particular importance is to ensure balanced distribution of aid relative to Muslims and Croats and the commission shall pay special attention to this." Mr. President, how do you look at this position of Prime Minister Lukic compared with the hearsay statement which you lent a lot of attention to, regardless of the hearsay aspect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These stances expressed here I welcome and I am very glad that we provided assistance in the implementation of these goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I offer both these documents to be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But I would like to reserve the right to perhaps at a later stage when we have a full translation of the document, to also request to add pages, if that is only now admitted in parts. But if it is admitted in full, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the size of the document, we'll admit them both in full. Shall we give the number? We'll mark them for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3060 and D3061 respectively MFI'd, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can you tell us from your experience what was the degree of accuracy of that information, that kind of information that reached you? To what degree did they prove to be wrong or correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well-known that the first casualty of every war is the truth. Intelligence and security services that cover and monitor every territory are not always slaves to the truth. They work for their own interests, but most often it is the only source of information. You have to work with that information although you could never swear that they are completely correct or truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions for Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless my colleagues have questions for you, Mr. Bulatovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the next witness is to be brought in the Chamber will issue an oral decision on the accused's motion to present testimony of General Stanislav Galic pursuant to Rule 92 ter filed on the 13th of February, 2013. In the motion the accused requests that the Chamber allows Stanislav Galic to testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter. On the 27th of February, 2013, the Prosecution responded to the motion. The Chamber recalls that on 21st of November, 2012, it found that it was in the interests of justice that Galic be called to testify viva voce. In reaching this decision the Chamber considered that Galic was commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the indictment period and that his evidence was central to the Sarajevo-related allegations. The Chamber further indicated that it was likely that a voluminous amount of material would be tendered through the witness. The Chamber, therefore, considers that the motion is a request for reconsideration of the Chamber's decision of the 21st of November, 2012. The accused argues in the motion that following the testimony of Dragomir Milosevic it is apparent that "more efficiency can be obtained without diminishing the ability of the Trial Chamber to evaluate the demeanour of the witness if Rule 92 ter is used." The Chamber is not satisfied that the viva voce testimony of Dragomir Milosevic demonstrates a clear error of reasoning on the Chamber's part in its decision of 21 November 2012 or that it is necessary to reconsider this decision in order to prevent an injustice. The Chamber shall, therefore, not reconsider its decision that Stanislav Galic be led live. There's one further matter, Mr. Robinson. On the 26th of February we received the file as your fourth revised witness list and we -- the Chamber noted that some additional witnesses have now been put in the "reserve list" category. So, for example, these include KW287, KW408, 424, 430. And I think, speaking for myself, this should have been done explicitly -- should have been -- was done with the explicit communication to the Chamber and the Prosecution, in particular given the length of the list and the various changes already made. So I would like you to identify the exhaustive list of those witnesses whose status was changed to reserve witness on the -- on this further revised 65 ter list. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Would you like me to do that orally right now or in a written pleading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would prefer a written submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this point, it would actually also be helpful that the Defence would make submissions when they revive someone from the reserve list; because, as we have seen, for the list for April there is a witness on there that was actually on the reserve. So he's now back active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So I think -- before doing this it should basically also be done in advance with a submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I need to supplement that slightly before Mr. Robinson rises, particularly noting the expression on his face when he heard the information to that effect. There is an explicit representation by the Defence that the placement of a witness on the reserve list means that witness will not be called, period. Now, reserving the situation of something very unusual in which there would be an explicit reason for doing so under exceptional circumstances, et cetera. And it's for that reason and based on that representation that the Prosecution didn't make specific applications to the Court concerning aspects of that issue. So I think Mr. Robinson will confirm that. I think that accounts for his -- what I understood from across the courtroom to be some surprise at the resurrection without any notice whatsoever, not to mention justification of a witness who had been placed on the reserve list. But I think that does need to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll have to look into that because I am surprised to learn that we've added someone from the reserve list. It's our position that when we place someone on the reserve list that we're representing to the Prosecution that they need not prepare for that witness. And if we want to -- if we intend to bring that witness, we're going to make an explicit notice to the Chamber and to the Prosecution and give them long lead time so that they can prepare. So I'll look into the situation with respect to that one witness and advise everyone as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next one is Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Samoukovic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Procedure and Evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question.
