But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please remember to pause between question and answer and to speak our sentences out slowly so that everything could be recorded in the transcript. Mr. Samoukovic, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 1D7819 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at the monitor. Do you see your statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you read and sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, can you make a longer pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness the last page so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom that were put to you then, would your answer in essence be the same as -- the answers in essence be the same as the ones in the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender this statement. I don't have any associated exhibits. I would like to submit this under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3062, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a brief summary of Mr. Nevenko Samoukovic's statement in English. [In English] Nevenko Samoukovic was elected president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici municipality. Mr. Nevenko Samoukovic is aware that the ethnic composition of Hadzici was predominantly Muslim. During the multi-party elections the SDS did not hold any promotional events in order to avoid irritating their Muslim and Croat neighbours, because the Serb population had been irritated by them. At these elections Mr. Nevenko Samoukovic was appointed chairman of the Executive Committee of Hadzici municipality. This committee consisted of six members, three Serbs and three Muslims, and in the beginning the committee functioned normally. Following these elections, the ethnic composition of managers in public and other enterprises did not correspond to the ethnic distribution of votes in the elections. As a consequence, the Muslims in authority tried to correct this; however, they were more concerned with the ethnic background of the person rather than their professional qualifications. This issue was especially acute after the referendum on the secession of BH from Yugoslavia and the declaration of an independent BH against the will of the Serbian people, who did not participate in the referendum. Nevenko Samoukovic considers that those in authority became increasingly unable to agree on various issues, both at the level of the Executive Committee and Municipal Assembly and at the level of the political parties; therefore, the municipal authorities were all but defunct. To compound this problem, the technical Remont company was located in the area of the municipality in addition to military barracks and facilities which housed large quantities of infantry and heavy weapons. Many Serbs were afraid that the Muslims would attack these facilities in order to get hold of the weapons. Mr. Nevenko Samoukovic is aware that during the period when the SDA and the SDS leaderships were discussing how to ease tensions and prevent chaos, but then the Muslims mounted their first armed attack on Hadzici and the joint authority ceased to function. Nevenko Samoukovic was not aware of the document called Variant A and B. The document was never mentioned at any of the meetings which he attended. When the armed conflict started, a Crisis Staff was created, the armed conflict was considered to be a sufficient extraordinary situation to establish the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff did not receive any directions or instructions from anyone, including central government. Further, there was an issue with communication because the telephone lines were down for the most part of the time. Nevenko Samoukovic believes that a large part of the Muslim population residing in Hadzici moved out voluntarily due to the situation and moved to the areas controlled by the Muslims. To his knowledge, no one in the territory of Hadzici made a decision to designate certain facilities as detention camps for Muslims. Certain facilities were used to house the remaining Muslim population to ensure their safety from uncontrolled groups or individuals. Muslim people who lived in Hadzici and were aware what Muslim forces were doing to Serb citizens feared reprisals. Many felt safer in the detention centre -- reception centre. Nevenko Samoukovic is aware that the war strategy for Hadzici was defensive in nature on the Serb side as the front line against the Muslims did not move until the end of the war. The Serbs in the municipality protected themselves and their homes. They did not have an objective to make conquests. Nevenko Samoukovic had not seen or heard Radovan Karadzic issue any kind of order to anyone in the area of the municipality of Hadzici. Nevenko Samoukovic is aware that Radovan Karadzic especially underlined that the authorities had to look after all of their citizens regardless of their nationality and party affiliation. He also emphasised that the authorities had to organise the production of food and other assets and ensure that the population and the army were supplied with the necessary provisions. Mr. Nevenko Samoukovic denies that there were any concentration camps in the territory of Hadzici. There were buildings where Muslims were temporarily placed to protect them from the uncontrolled groups. He was aware that the police station used one of its rooms for the purposes of detention, but only for perpetrators of criminal offences. He had heard that one prison existed and other buildings were used as detention areas as they were in municipal buildings; however, he denies that there were ever any concentration camps in municipality of Hadzici under the Serb control. [Interpretation] This is a brief summary and at this point I don't have any more questions for Mr. Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Samoukovic, as you have noted, your evidence in this case was -- evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, i.e., your -- through your written statement. And now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd first like to focus briefly on the period prior to the conflict breaking out. Now, during this period you were still the chairman of the Executive Committee of Hadzici. At paragraph 9 of your statement you say that the president of the SDS in the municipality of Hadzici was the late Ratko Radic. And you state that it was largely the political leaders of the party who conduct negotiations all the time about how to ease the tensions in such a chaotic situation arising from a non-functioning Assembly. Now, Mr. Samoukovic, there's evidence before the Trial Chamber that Ratko Radic stated at multi-party meetings in January 1992 that the Serbs didn't want to be in Alija's state and that separation and division was necessary and unavoidable. Now, would you agree that expressing such a view was unlikely to ease the tensions in this situation?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: With a yes and a no. Are you asking me to answer with a yes or a no? Can you please explain to me what you mean by the words "Alija's state"? Bosnia and Herzegovina always in modern history functioned as a state comprising three peoples. The main principle, the basic principle, in the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina during World War II was the second anti-fascist council of Bosnia and Herzegovina session which stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina was not Serb, Croat, or Muslim, but it was Serb and Croat and Muslim. And every child in elementary school that did not know that definition would fail their history class. Ratko Radic said that he did not want to live in Alija's state. I think I understood you correctly that you said he did not want to live in Alija's state, which probably implied that he did not wish to live in a state in which one people would dominate another people. So this is a principle in opposition to the founding principles of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Muslims also used to say that they did not want to live in Milosevic's Yugoslavia. So that is how that statement should be taken, meaning that he did not wish to live in a state where one people would dominate the other two people, and the purpose was to say that we have to agree to live in a place where all three peoples would respect each other and where all three peoples would have their own rights, not that one people would dominate another.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samoukovic. We'll come onto that further. But in your statement, paragraph 10, you explain that you resigned from your position as chairman of the Executive Committee of the municipality at the beginning of May. And at paragraph 18 you explain that when the conflict began in Hadzici around the 10th of May you were home sick, so not up-to-date with many events that took place at the time. Were you aware that on the 8th of May a group of armed Serbs had entered the Hadzici municipality building, expelling all the workers and taking over the building?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "no," not "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And did you attend a multi-party meeting between key municipality members on the afternoon of the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, again, Mr. Samoukovic, there is evidence before the Trial Chamber - and that's for the parties' reference at P41, Ramiz Dupovac's evidence - that Radic conducted -- concluded that meeting by threatening that unless a resolution was reached there would be blood deep up to the knees. Again, would you agree that this type of language would be unlikely to ease the heightened tension of this time?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please repeat your question. Perhaps the translation is not good. I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Radic at a meeting of -- on the 8th of May stated that unless a resolution was reached there would be blood deep up to the knees. Now, my question for you is: This -- using this type of language was unlikely to ease the tensions that were prevailing at this time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic was - let me put it this way - a man who completed craftsman's education. So the way he expressed himself was something that was a consequence of his broadness of mind and education. I don't know what the other side was saying in this instance. Was there some kind of polemic or -- I don't know. I don't have complete insight. I wasn't present at the meeting so I don't know what each of the sides was saying. But in principle, I know that all of those meetings that were held before were quite quarrelsome. They did try, but actually they did not reach any kind of solution at any of the meetings. It wasn't just Mr. Radic, but it was the president of the municipality who usually chaired those meetings. He was an educated man, but he wasn't a politically educated man, in the sense that he was never involved in politics. So he didn't know how to conduct these meetings. He would go straight for the heart of the problem and then there would be a quarrel breaking out right at the start of the meeting so that party representatives would then leave the meetings and they would leave the meeting even after a third of it -- after one-third of it had gone on because they could tell how the meeting would continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samoukovic. I was just waiting for the end of the translation. I'm going to move on to a different topic and I'll ask you to focus -- to try to give answers that are as concise and precise as possible. Thank you. At paragraph 22 of your statement you say that you have -- you had not heard or seen Radovan Karadzic issue any kind of order to anyone in the area of the municipality of Hadzici. Now, the Assembly of the Serbian people of Hadzici at its session of 11th April 1992 constituted the organs and the bodies of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Hadzici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And at the Assembly you were given a mandate to form the municipal government; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And also at this Assembly a decision was adopted to establish a Serbian police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: There are minutes and if it's in the minutes then probably that's so. I don't remember the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: For the parties' reference the minutes to this meeting are D2916 and it is indeed in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Samoukovic, just over two weeks previously, on the 24th of March, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina held their 12th Session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I could have P961, please, which is a stenograph of this meeting. And I'm interested in page 22 of the English and page 39 of the B/C/S. And if I can direct the parties' attention to the fifth paragraph -- the large paragraph in the English version -- obviously the large paragraph in both versions. And I'm just going to read an extract from this which is a statement by Dr. Karadzic who says: "We have a legal basis in the Law on Internal Affairs and we also have the insignia and at a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days. Such are the forecasts, but I can't tell you the reasons now. At that moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned." And then shortly after he continues: "Then at a given moment in the next three or four days, there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, including both things that must be done as well as how to do them, how to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Samoukovic, this statement was made by Dr. Karadzic just over two weeks previously to the Hadzici Assembly, setting up its own bodies and its own police station. So, in fact, the very decision to constitute that Assembly and to separate the police force was taken pursuant to a directive by Mr. Karadzic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: When the Crisis Staff was formed, it took over the work of the Assembly and its organs and services; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you state at paragraph 14 that the Crisis Staff had around 15 to 20 members and was made up of the most influential and most capable people, regardless of their party affiliation. Just to clarify, by this do you mean the most capable and influential Serbs regardless of their affiliation to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: By that I mean capable and influential persons, those who wanted to work voluntarily. For example, I'm a member of the Crisis Staff. A moment ago you said that I was elected president of the municipal government, and in the Crisis Staff I did the work for which I was best fitted. Since I'm a civil engineer, I worked in that field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We understand that point. My question is simply just clarifying when you say that it was made up of people regardless of their party affiliation, do you mean it was made up of Serb people regardless of their affiliation to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course the party affiliation did not matter at that point at all. All those who expressed the goodwill and wish to help in that situation was welcome. If I tell you that in the Crisis Staff we had an elderly man who was only in charge of funerals, his job was funerals only, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let me make my question even simpler. Were there any non-Serbs on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, at least not from that point in time when I came to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And in paragraph 14 you also state that the Crisis Staff did not receive any directions or instructions from anyone, including the central government, and you worked independently. And further at paragraph 22 you state that even if you needed to get in touch with someone from the Presidency or the government in Pale, you couldn't do it because the telephone lines were torn. I'd like to look now at some documents regarding communications between the Hadzici authorities and the central government and Presidency. If we could have P2625, please. Now, Mr. Samoukovic, these are minutes of a meeting of the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 18th of May, 1992. I'd like to turn to pages 2 in the English and Bosnian -- B/C/S versions, please. And at "Ad-2," so at the bottom of the page in English and B/C/S it states that: "It was concluded that aid be given to the Novo Sarajevo and Hadzici Crisis Staffs and that the amount of aid be determined according to the situation in these municipalities." So it's clear from this document, isn't it, that by that stage the government was aware that the Crisis Staff had been set up?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The document shows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the document also suggests that the government was informed of the situation in the Hadzici municipality, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: How they were informed, I don't know, but if it is stated here that we need help - and indeed we did need help - they probably had ways of finding out. But telephones only operated locally, within the municipality, the part that was covered by our telephone exchange because our transmitter went through Sarajevo. So technically it was impossible for us to have some kind of communication. We could communicate with the city, with Sarajevo. We actually had two or three lines via railway telephones with the other side in Sarajevo and certain contacts were made later on with the other side through those telephones regarding population exchanges and so on. However, telephone lines with Pale, we didn't have them. We did in 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: -- when our passive transmitter was turned towards Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The interprets have asked that you speak a little closer to the microphone. But we're going to continue on this topic of communications between the Hadzici authorities and the republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 1548.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, you'll see that this is a letter from Republika Srpska government secretary Nedeljko Lakic to Romanija Petrol dated the 28th of May, 1992, and he's asking Romanija Petrol to deliver 50 litres of fuel to the Crisis Staff from Hadzici and to bill it to the Government of the Serbian Republic of BiH. So you'll agree that this shows the government intervening to give material support to the Hadzici Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree. If 50 litres is assistance, well this is probably some individual who was up there in Pale and who introduced himself as having some kind of connections with Hadzici in order to get 50 litres of fuel. I mean, what kind of aid is that, 50 litres of fuel? I'm sure that it must be some individual who was up there in Pale, who perhaps went for medical treatment or something, went there with his family, introduced himself as a member of the Crisis Staff, that that would be assistance to the Crisis Staff, 50 litres, no, surely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Samoukovic, we'll come on to further assistance to the Crisis Staff very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could I please have Exhibit D317.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, this is a report on combat-readiness of the Serb municipality of Hadzici to the SRK command dated the 29th of May, 1992. And I'd like to focus your discussion -- or focus your attention, rather, on the discussion which is halfway down the page in the English and I believe at the lower end of the page in the B/C/S, if we could scroll down a little -- oh, maybe it's the second page in the B/C/S. But just to explain, this is a discussion of an attack on Zunovica barracks on the 25th of May, 1992, and it states: "Combat activities were not favourable for us, so the Crisis Staff of Serb municipality of Hadzici asked assistance from defenders of MRD Hadzici." It continues: "We asked for help from the commander of the HQ of the Serb Republic of BiH himself, who presently sent a fighting group under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic Milisav, who after he arrived at the location where the fighting was in progress, organised available men, suspended the attack of Ustasha, and held them on the line that separates two-thirds of Zunovica storage premises." Mr. Samoukovic, do you recall this request for help?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you will have to move a little closer to the microphone. The interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You will agree that this document shows the Hadzici Crisis Staff contacting the highest level of republican authorities for help.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Hadzici asked assistance from the maintenance and repair depot in Hadzici -- it's in Hadzici. We didn't ask for assistance in Pale. We asked for assistance in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Samoukovic, the document says: "We asked for help from the commander of the HQ of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina himself." So again I'll ask you: Do you agree that this shows the Hadzici Crisis Staff contacting the republican authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Who asked for that? It was the maintenance and repair depot. This is a report from someone at that institution and he says here unequivocally that they were the ones who asked for help.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'll move on to a different document, which is P3087. Now, these are minutes from the 26th government meeting of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 11th of June, 1992. And you'll note that on the first page the agenda item -- I'm sorry, it's on the second page of the B/C/S version. Agenda item number 9 is: "Request for giving loans to municipalities." If we can skip forward to page 4 of the English and B/C/S version, please. It states that, "The Decision regarding" -- I'm sorry, this is at number 9. It states that: "The Decision regarding loans from the reserves of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been made to the municipality of Vlasenica 2.500.000 and to Hadzici 1.040.000 dinars." So once again here you agree that we see assistance being provided from the government to Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And just one final document on this topic, which is P3064. These are minutes of the 8th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 17th of June, 1992. And you'll see that president -- present, rather, are Dr. Karadzic and the other Presidency members. And if you look at the second paragraph in the document, or rather, the third paragraph it states: "The Presidency was briefed on the situation on the front, particularly in Ilijas and Hadzici where enemy forces viciously attacked our army positions the day before, and once again, as many times before, violated the truce." So again, this shows that -- it shows that Republika Srpska Presidency being well informed of operations in and around Hadzici, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that since this had to do with the 25th of May, the 10th of June, the 16th of June, Hadzici was exposed to constant attacks. That was a fact. Those who were involved in military matters knew about that. This is an undeniable fact. This information certainly went up there; that is to say that we were exposed to constant attacks. And probably that assistance that we spoke about a moment ago had to do with these constant attacks and the threats to the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But it's a fact, isn't it, Mr. Samoukovic, that many communications took place between the republican authorities and the Hadzici municipality -- municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal authorities, well I'm saying what kind of communication we had. Now, whether the army had their own types of communication, I mean, probably they did. What kind of an army would it be otherwise? And after all that is something different of course. I don't know about that. I'm not that knowledgeable about these technical matters, but I assume they did have something like that, because this also speaks about attacks. This also has to do with military reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's turn then to your specific role as a Crisis Staff member. In paragraph 12 of your statement you describe the various tasks that you had a Crisis Staff member and you explained that you worked on -- one of the tasks was working on the protection of property, taking care of the abandoned apartments, which in the vast majority belonged to Muslims, and making a list of those apartments in order to seal and secure them. Now, you were appointed by Crisis Staff president, Ratko Radic, to -- as a member of a commission to make a list of all abandoned flats and property on the territory of Hadzici municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And actually if we may have D1084, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is your appointment -- or rather, Mr. Radic's decision to form the commission in which you're appointed. And he states: "The appointed commission is obliged to make a list of all abandoned flats and property on the territory of Hadzici Serb Municipality and also to seal them so they could be registered and placed at the disposal of Hadzici Serb Municipality." Now, by placing them at the disposal of the municipality, this meant that the municipality could allocate those apartments to Serbs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The question is allocate in which sense? Well, look, this sentence here is be made available to the Serb municipality of Hadzici. I remember that full well. We had this discussion as to why it was included at all. It was put there because a commission had been established to register these apartments, to seal them, and to prevent looting, and that is why this sentence was included, so that it would be well-known that the authorities are standing behind these lists of property and the authorities would not allow those kind of things to happen. And these apartments afterwards, when the refugees arrived from Tarcin, Pazarici, and other places, these apartments were temporarily being given to these refugees for their use.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to look at P739, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is on the same topic. It's a letter from Dr. Karadzic dated the 19th of July, 1992, to Sarajevo municipalities, including Hadzici. And Dr. Karadzic says: "In close co-operation with public security stations, you are kindly requested to make an inventory of all housing facilities (summer cottages, houses, and flats) in your municipality that are vacant following the voluntary departure of Muslims." And he states that: "Pursuant to the Presidency's decision ... these facilities will be given for temporary use to Serbs from the Muslim part of Sarajevo." Now, Hadzici authorities received this instruction and acted upon it, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Our activity took place two months before this instruction. Two months before this instruction we immediately registered this property in order to seal it, protect it, et cetera. This instruction is from the month of July and that decision of the Crisis Staff is from May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter number 24665.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Samoukovic, this is a letter dated just over one week later, that's the 27th of July, 1992, from the municipal secretariat for housing and public utilities signed by you as secretary to the commissioners of the Serbian municipality Hadzici. And in it you ask that they inventory all abandoned and vacant buildings that can be lived in and all vacant weekend houses that can be lived in. Now, in requesting this list to be made you were acting on the instructions of Dr. Karadzic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Number one, I did not sign this. Here it says "on behalf of the secretary," "for the secretary," and down here this is not my signature. So, I mean, this document is unknown to me and you can see that it says here "for." Somebody signed this on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, you will agree that the -- whoever -- whichever representative of the Hadzici authorities who signed it on your behalf was acting on the instructions of Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Up here, take a look at the heading. It says "Serb municipality of Hadzici, municipal secretariat." There is no more Crisis Staff. There is a municipal government and secretariats that dealt with particular fields. Now, whether this was done in accordance with this -- well, it's illogical for someone to come from Sarajevo to Hadzici and for somebody in Hadzici to provide accommodation to people from Sarajevo. That's illogical. That did not happen. There was not a single case of that kind. Organs of government are already functioning here. It is possible that there was some communication where the government did something or -- but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, just if I could just offer one reserve. I'm just trying to check with Mr. Reid if this had been disclosed to us earlier, but pending that we don't have any objection at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see that number in the notice, but it is -- -- disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was an earlier disclosure obligation, but it may very well have been disclosed to us. I didn't have time to check myself and I asked Mr. Reid who is very quick at that. So I'll get that information soon, but in the meantime we can admit it. If there's a problem I'll raise it with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you coming to a conclusion, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one additional topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would it take?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: May I just -- your indulgence while I check how much time I have left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I can finish in five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do so, yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Turning a totally different topic, Mr. Samoukovic, you explained in your statement that there were no concentration camps in the territory of Hadzici, but rather areas where Muslims were temporarily placed to protect them. And you state that Muslim people would go to the reception centre willingly and seek opportunities to leave their territory. Now, there is evidence before the Trial Chamber from witnesses who were unwillingly taken to Hadzici sports centre - and that's P161, P2403, for the parties' reference - including a witness who was under house arrest until 16th May 1992 when he was taken to the sports centre and witnesses -- a witness who testified that between 25th of May and June -- 22nd of June, there were 282 people detained in the sports hall. Now, these people didn't actually express a wish to be held in the sports centre, did they?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot answer whether they did or did not express their wishes because none of them approached me nor did I have any conversations with any of them, so I cannot answer that question. As far as I know --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, SJB commander, Glavas, who was a fellow member of the Crisis Staff testified that people were taken from their houses by the TO and the police. Were you aware of this occurring?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that the police brought in some people and took them from their houses. I heard about that. The police had their reasons why they do things. They probably had some operative intelligence. And in the police, like in every profession, there are incompetent people who are not professionals, those who abuse their position and powers. But the fact is some of them have already been prosecuted for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, it was Mr. Glavas' evidence that the decision was made by the Crisis Staff that all Bosniak men of military age were to be arrested and detained from areas such as Binjezevo, Zunovica and Kucice. Now, you've already stated that you weren't around at that period, but do you agree that it's correct that only the Crisis Staff had the authority to make this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get a reference and an exact quotation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My apologies. That was an exact quotation and it's from P2296, paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question, Mr. Samoukovic? Do you agree -- or Mr. Glavas testified that a decision was made by the Crisis Staff to arrest Bosniak men of military age and detain them. Do you agree that --

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In my own statement I said as far as I know the Crisis Staff never made such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: They never made such a decision to your knowledge, but you agree that the Crisis Staff were the authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was a body responsible for the situation on the ground to the extent the Crisis Staff was able to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, given the pace of hearing today, I take it there would be no point of holding General Vasiljevic in the waiting room anymore?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I think that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Samoukovic, you were asked when the Serbian municipality of Hadzici was formed. Are you able to tell us what comprised the Serbian municipality of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian -- in what sense when was it formed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 58 you were asked if it was formed on the 12th, or whichever, April. I'm not asking you when it was formed. I'm just asking you what that area comprised, what made up that municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Hadzici Serbian municipality didn't have any territory. It was a political formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out, what did the Serbian authorities control of the Serbian municipality of Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: A few days after the combat erupted, when the lines of defence were established, we controlled perhaps some 15 to 20 per cent of the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the majority population on the territory under your control?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there a Muslim municipality also in the territory of the Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they have a Crisis Staff and later the organs of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked if there were any Muslims in the Serbian Crisis Staff. Were there any Serbs in the Muslim Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that as far as I knew there were no Muslims in our staff and as far as I know there were no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you say after as far as you know there were ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were no Muslim in ours. What about Serbs in theirs?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were none?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Crisis Staff or the unit plan and execute offensive actions with the intention of capturing this Muslim part of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The lines of separation that were established in the course of May and June held until the end of the war practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D13021.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see whether this is a document confirming that the Muslims had their own Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you know the president of the Crisis Staff, Mustafa Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of the municipality and I was the president of the Executive Board before the war time events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd just like to interject here that the Muslim Crisis Staff was not the focus of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was wondering myself how it did arise from the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, Madam McKenna created the impression that there was no division of power in the municipality so that one would expect that there were Muslims in the Serbian Crisis Staff and that the Muslims did not have their own authority or their Crisis Staff. Page 60 of today's transcript, line 12, is where it is stated: Why didn't you have any Muslims? As if the Muslims were stripped of all of their rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may, I believe Mr. Karadzic is referring to the line of questioning which was simply to clarify the witness's assertion in his statement that the Crisis Staff was comprised of people regardless of party affiliation. I am simply clarifying what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, she didn't deal with the division of Hadzici at all. Why don't you move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, it was implied that this was in terms of ethnic belonging, but the witness was talking about party affiliation and the question was that the Muslims were not included in the Serbian Crisis Staff but, however, they had their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, witness testified that so you don't need further evidence. Why don't you move on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I just wanted to corroborate. Are you going to admit the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 56 you were told that Ramiz Dupovac testified here and in his testimony he conveyed the words of Ratko Radic. I did not cross-examine Dupovac because the statement was submitted under a different Rule. Did you know Ramiz Dupovac?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what he is, what is he like and what did he do?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he take part in the war afterwards?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the communications between the government and the central organs. Are you saying that you were completely isolated or that your daily communications were reduced?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Our daily communications were reduced. Let me explain. The communication towards Pale was a physical one. So if somebody was daring enough, could go through some forests and in areas hard to pass to communicate and those people were shot at. I dared to go on that trip with my sister and her husband, and her husband was left without a leg and we were forced to take him to Belgrade after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D1072, please. It's a Defence exhibit, D1072. This is a report on the work of the defence ministry Hadzici office. Can we look at page 5 now, please -- 4, it's page 4 in the English and it's page 5 in the Serbian. At the end of -- at the bottom of the page in the English -- actually, we also need page 5 in the Serbian. [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would now like to present a paragraph to you. In English I think it beginnings with the words "we tried to establish necessary co-operation ...": I'm going to read it in Serbian: "Co-operation by means of various letters, requests, orders, and even visits to the Presidency of the republic and the General Staff of the army but without success. In mid-September, however, we managed to break through the barrier and establish co-operation which is today at an enviable level." How does this tally with your experiences and knowledge about the defence department's problems and what they state are their problems?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's just as I told you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Text was quoted to you from Mr. Glavas' statement and I would like to give you a more complete citation from that in the Serbian, and they can translate it: [In English] "Document undated report on the work of the Assembly of the Serb municipality of Hadzici in 1992. It has been ERN of 0228-7570 to 7571. "I can say that I have never seen this report before; however, I can see mention of December of 1992 the municipality is being organised and various organs are functioning. It says in this document the Crisis Staff took over complete supervision of the Assembly and its organs and services." [Interpretation] Are you able to tell us when the Municipal Assembly and the Assembly board and the Crisis Staff worked together at any point in time? Did the Crisis Staff take over control over the Municipal Assembly at the parliament session?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, the Crisis Staff did all the functions. The Assembly never convened. It was only in July, I think we saw it from the documents that the Madam Prosecutor showed and at the heading they're talking about the secretariats, meaning when the Executive Board was formed, the secretariats after that, then the Assembly began its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Staff continue to function?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. With the cessation of the operation of the Assembly, then the war time organs began to work such as the municipal Executive Board and the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the cessation of the work of the Crisis Staff or the municipality? We just want to clarify a possible error?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: With the cessation of the operation of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What continued?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Then the organs of authority, such as the Executive Board and the Assembly, were established. And as far as I can remember, this was in the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 70, 71, you were asked about concentration camps - moving on to a completely different topic - and how you said that they came to the reception centre of their own free will in order to seek shelter until they left for their territory. And then it was said that -- what was said about Glavas. The question the way it was put -- I'm going to read it out so it can be properly translated: [In English] "Q. Well, SJB commander, Glavas, who was a fellow member of the Crisis Staff testified that people were taken from their houses by the Territorial Defence and the police. Were you aware of this occurring?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "A. I knew that the police brought in some people and took them from their houses. I heard about that. The police had their reasons why they do things. They probably had some operative intelligence. And in the police, like in every profession, there are incompetent people who are not professionals, those are abuse their positions, position of power. But the fact is some of them have already been prosecuted for that." [Interpretation] Now I would like to show you what the commander of the public security station, Mr. Glavas, was writing at that time. Can we look at D1074. And while we're waiting, are you able to tell us where those who were in police detention at the police building were going, what was the outcome? What could have happened to them after their interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably prison or reception centre, some probably home also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to read a report to the security centre dated the 9th of August, 1992. It states: "Upon the establishment of the Serbian police station of Hadzici, i.e., in the phase of its formation as well as over the next 40 or so days, the activities of certain small groups so-called 'free shooters' was noted ..." And then a little bit lower it says: "This police station, among other things, the execution of tasks and assignments was approached with due seriousness, primarily security, protection of the legal and property, safety of the citizens, maintaining of law and order, as well as the prevention and uncovering of crimes and their perpetrators." How does this fit in with your understanding of the work of the police at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it corresponds to my answer, but I do want to say that the police -- there were few of them and they really could not manage to cover and carry out all of their duties and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the last page of the document? It's the one-page-but-last in the English. I'm also going to read a part of paragraph (d): "As regards the procedure and jurisdiction in connection with the treatment and guarding of prisoners, it can be noted that we had a large number of detained persons who, once they were interviewed and after other relevant information had been gathered, were taken to state prison in Kula or were released. A small number of people brought in (currently 11 persons) are in prison in Hadzici and they are being treated properly and in accordance with the law. "We would also like to know that in the area of the Hadzici municipality we do not have collection camps used by the army to bring in the Muslim population without documents on the reasons for their detention." How does this fit in with your knowledge and experience about the legality of the operation of the police?

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the Crisis Staff as far as I know, I probably would have heard of it or seen it, never adopted any decisions on the formation of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not make out the rest of the sentence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Samoukovic, for answering my questions and thank you for behaving professionally during the war and everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters didn't catch your last answer. If you remember, could you repeat it? What we have at the moment is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that is stated in this report is in accordance and is not in collision with what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you say? The Crisis Staff never adopted any decision on the formation of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it is written somewhere here -- please help me, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the statement.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: Camps are mentioned somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this report, (d), point (d), the last page and then the second photograph: "We also emphasise that in the area of Hadzici municipality there are no collection camps where the army is bringing Muslim population without any documents on the reason why they are brought in." Can you then explain what you said about the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: NEVENKO SAMOUKOVIC
utterances.text: What I've already stated, that the Crisis Staff never made such a decision and that this report of Mr. Glavas is consistent with my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That then concludes your evidence, Mr. Samoukovic. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling in relation to the testimony of Obren Markovic and Tomislav Puhalac. First, having reviewed the proposed Rule 92 ter statement for Obren Markovic, the Chamber finds that the following portions contain detailed information not relevant to the crimes in the indictment. These are paragraphs 6, the last sentence of paragraph 21, paragraphs 27 from "I know during these bombardments," and paragraph 32 from "an example of such crimes" until "I am saying this because after the crime." Next, having also reviewed the proposed Rule 92 ter statement for Tomislav Puhalac, the Chamber finds that paragraph 19 contains detailed information not relevant to the crimes in the indictment. The Chamber therefore decides that the aforementioned paragraphs and the documents included therein shall be redacted from the respective Rule 92 ter statements and orders that redacted versions be uploaded onto e-court prior to the witness's testimony. The Chamber also encourages the accused with respect to the evidence he proposes to lead on Brcko to be mindful that the indictment only alleges responsibility for crimes purported to have been committed in Luka camp and to focus his attention on his alleged responsibility for those crimes. Let's bring in the next witness. I would very much like to conclude next witness for today so please bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic and Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will do its utmost and the Prosecution too, I believe. But as far as the previous decision is concerned, I'm not disputing it but I want to express my concern for the record that the case file will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- will lack context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tolj. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Tolj, I would like to draw your attention to a certain Rule of Procedure and Evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule you may object to answering a question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you. In this context "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal will ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolj. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tolj.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation and I would like you to do the same. Please do not start answering until the cursor stops.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for 1D7818 to be displayed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read this statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please hold your answers for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please display the last page for the witness to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect everything you've said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same as here in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: They would be essentially the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I tender these statements under 92 ter without any associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3063, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to read a brief summary of Mr. Mladen Tolj's statement in English. [In English] Mr. Mladen Tolj was appointed chief of the SJB Hadzici in 1992. He states that after the multi-party election he could feel the division between the Serbs and the Muslims in both the town and the station. Due to this, a large number of policemen left the station and Muslim [sic] reservists were drafted in to fill these gaps. Mladen Tolj recalls that one day when the members of the Green Berets came to the station and informed the police that the Serbs would shell the police station so Green Berets had come to evacuate the official vehicles and other equipment. They then took this equipment and drove the vehicles away. Mladen Tolj did not return to work after this incident. Mladen Tolj went to register for work at the Hadzici police station; however, he noted that there was not a single Serb working there as the station had already been divided ethnically. Later he received an invitation to join the Serbian Hadzici police which was located at the premises of the construction company above the post office. To begin with, co-operation with the Muslims was good -- at the beginning the co-operation with the Muslims was good and the joint check-points and patrols were set up. Mladen Tolj cannot remember the exact date when the Muslim forces began shelling Hadzici; however, women, children, and elderly were quickly evacuated. A part of the Muslim population who expressed such a wish were housed in the gym at the secondary school to be protected. This was not a camp but temporary accommodation. Transport was arranged for the Muslims who so wanted to travel to the Muslim-controlled area. Mr. Mladen Tolj is aware of one incident at the gym when the Muslims were -- where the Muslims were housed there when a group of Serbs entered without authorisation and maltreated the people they found there. Following this, a further group of Muslims expressed the wish to leave Hadzici and transport was once again arranged. This incident was in response to the Serb population in Hadzici discovering that the Muslims were torturing the Serb civilians, their relatives, at the school -- at the Silos camp. At the beginning of the war, a large number of Serbs were taken to the Silos camp and beaten and tortured. Some were kept until the camp until 1996. The municipal authorities allowed Muslims to leave Hadzici without hindrance as often as possible. Mladen Tolj would not consider any of the camps alleged to exist by the Muslims to be camps. A temporary holding centre for the Muslims existed which provided accommodation until they were transported from Hadzici. A detention space existed for military conscripts who had had a run-in with the law. Other premises were used whilst the situation [sic] were being located from one building to another. Mladen Tolj is not aware of any murders in any of these premises. In relation to his work every person, regardless of ethnicity, when brought to the police station were registered with the appropriate records. The police in Hadzici did not receive all of their orders from the political leadership in Pale municipality as the police had neither the time nor the ability to contact anyone. The telephone lines were down more often than they worked. Further, Hadzici municipality was physically cut off from Pale as the Muslims had cut off the roads. And that is the summary, and I think I made mistake that Muslim reserves were drafted. I think it was Serbian reservists were drafted to fill these gaps in the army. No questions for this witness for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tolj, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tolj.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At paragraph 15 of your statement you state that you were appointed commander of the Hadzici police station at some point during autumn 1992. I'd like to show you 65 ter 24575, please. So in this document which is dated 17th August, 1992, the Hadzici municipality Executive Council recommends to the Ministry of the Interior in Pale that you be appointed commander of SJB Hadzici. So you were appointed by the Ministry of the Interior following this recommendation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 13 of your statement you mention a number of detention centres and you also describe how all the people detained were registered with the appropriate records in your statement. Now, under the criminal code in force at the time, it's correct, isn't it, that the police were authorised to issue a detention on custody that could last up to three days.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And the code of criminal procedure also stipulated that at the end of that three-day period police forces had an obligation to bring the detainee before an investigative judge, who would then issue a decision on continued custody or release; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, I'd first like to focus on the detention centre in the garage in the municipality building. Non-Serbs were arrested and brought in to be interviewed by the police in the municipality building premises; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: The Muslim population was brought in not only by the police but also by army units from combat. They were not only rounded up in houses. They were brought in also from combat zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that included the people captured in the attack by your police force on the village of Musici, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I could not give you a specific answer regarding Musici village because I was not at the police station at the time. I was on the lines in position on one of the lines. I believe it was done by a combined unit consisting of police officers and military police officers; they carried out that attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that 40 men from Musici were brought to the municipality building garage after the attack. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And while they were detained in the garage, you and other members of the police interrogated them in the office upstairs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You frequently worked together with Zoran Gasevic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: We were sent on missions together quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, you agree that the garage in which the detainees were held was a small concrete garage?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: That was a garage in the ownership of the Municipal Assembly of Hadzici, where a number of vehicles were kept as well as archives that were kept in one part of the garage, and there was also plumbing inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But at one time around 50 people were held there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the number because it fluctuated. Some people were transferred to the gym usually when there was fighting. If some people were captured in the fighting, they would be brought to the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, in the garage on occasion men and women were held together; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I believe there were one or two such cases, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The detainees had no means of cleaning themselves, did they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: For hygiene they had the same facilities as everybody else because in Hadzici we did not have either water or electricity for a while because the Muslim side had cut off the supply. It was a huge problem for the entire population of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about your obligations in relation to those detainees. You've agreed that the police were permitted to detain people for three-day period, and after which they were required to bring the detainee before an investigative judge. So that should have been what you did in respect of those detained in the Hadzici municipality building, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: In the building of Hadzici municipality, Ilidza, Ilijas, et cetera, there was no courthouse, so there was no possibility for these people to be turned over to the proper authorities for further procedure. Communications towards Pale, Lukavica, and other places were cut off. You could reach them only taking tracks through woods and that was dangerous because every now and then there were raids by various groups and even some of our policemen got killed or injured in that way when they were intercepted by Muslim army units on those roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tolj, I'd like to focus on the issue of the detainees under -- in your custody in the municipality building. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence - and that's at P2403 at paragraphs 48 and 51 - that men from Musici were held there for six days. It's also heard evidence that people were held there for weeks, including one group for as long as 33 days, and that's at paragraph 66 of P2403. Now, this is detention far beyond permissible detention under the law in force at the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I agree, but if you understood my previous answer I said that there were war operations engulfing the whole area. It was not possible to transport people into proper premises before the competent organs that would take charge from then on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, these people never received a decision on detention by any authority in accordance with the law in force at the time, did they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I believe so because - and I think I've said this before - the police station was based on the premises in the offices of a construction company. So we came in without any equipment, without any communications equipment, without any amenities or proper facilities for police work. We had no proper premises or equipment, and most policemen, sometimes 100 per cent of them, were engaged to hold the lines and had no time to do their job, which was police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tolj, I'll ask you to listen carefully to the question that I'm asking and to respond as accurately and as concisely as possible. We have very little time. Let's come back to the interviews of the detainees. Now, after the interviews some of the people who you had determined didn't pose a threat would be transferred to the sports centre?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Roughly that's right. People on whom no weapons were found were taken to the sports centre because that was the safest place for them because of various raids by groups out of control, people who were under nobody's command, people who were not within the police or the army system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's then focus on the sports centre now. At paragraph 9 of your statement you say that a part of the Muslim population who had expressed such a wish were put up in arrangement with them at the gym of the secondary school centre so they would be protected. And you continue -- you also state that after a while the Muslims who so wanted were transported by buses to the side under the control of their people, that is to say Kiseljak. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard -- well, you've just accepted that people who were taken to the sports centre from the municipality building garages following their interviews -- is it your evidence that these people asked to be taken to the sports centre from the municipal garage?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the ending because I'm not sure I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tolj, in paragraph 9 of your statement you suggest that the people were taken -- or people went to the sports centre voluntarily. I'm asking you whether it is your position that the people who were taken to the sports centre after their interviews by your police in the municipality building garage -- or in the municipality building, did those people go to the sports centre voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Very few went voluntarily. Most were brought there and kept there with the best of intentions because that's where it was the safest for them. There were cases when people were allowed to go home because that was their wish. They would spend even less than 24 hours at home and an incident would occur. They would be attacked and then they would reappear, or rather, there would be these people who did whatever they wanted as they roamed about, so then these people would return to the centre because they felt safest there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, it was the public security centre who was responsible for the organisation and security of the sports centre, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Not the public security centre. It was the army, or rather, mobilisation. And it was the military authorities that provided security for the entire centre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript. [Interpretation] In line 10 of the transcript it doesn't say that yet again these people who freely roamed about and would mistreat other people, it wasn't recorded in line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 10 of your statement you describe how after Serbs broke into the gym and mistreated the people there, the political and military leadership made the decision to transport part of the Muslims at their own request from the gym to the Muslim-controlled side at Kiseljak while the remainder was transported to the Kula prison, that is, those who had violated the law. Now, it was Mr. Glavas's evidence, your predecessor as SJB commander, that the Crisis Staff president Ratko Radic gave the order to transfer 180 to 200 detainees to the Kula prison on the 22nd of June, 1992. For the parties' reference that's P2296, paragraph 50, and T11785 to 6. Mr. Tolj, is it your position that all 200 of these people being transferred to Kula prison had violated the law?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I am not of the view that all of them had violated the law. Quite simply, the order was that they could no longer be held in detention on the premises where they had been until then.
