They had to be transferred to institutions, prisons, that were envisaged for that, and then of course that the procedure was continue over there and everything else. And as far as I know, immediately after being transferred to the Kula prison some people were immediately released and they went to the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence from people who were part of that transfer, Witnesses Mehmet Music and Adem Balic, who were transferred from the sports centre to Kula prison and held there until they were transferred to further detention centres. So rather than being voluntarily bussed to Kiseljak, as your statement suggests, these detainees were being transferred from detention centre to detention centre; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I really don't know of the fate of individual persons who were transferred to Kula prison and how they were then transferred from there, how many were released, how many were transferred to other prisoners. That was very hard for us to control, or rather, to have information. The road we used from Lukavica to Hadzici was over 100 kilometres long, round about, over the hills. Telephone lines weren't working either so communication was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about those people who were being held in the sports centre during the period in which you were SJB commander. It's correct, isn't it, Mr. Tolj, that non-Serbs were held in the sports centre right up until October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Well, in that period I was appointed commander and that's where I found them. Perhaps there were about then persons there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P1607 and page 2 in the English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tolj, this is a report on the situation in prisons and collection camps for prisoners of war from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Justice and administration representative, Slobodan Avlijas. I'd like to turn to section 10 on Hadzici, that's English page 6 to 7 and B/C/S page 5. And I should have noted, Mr. Tolj, that the date of this document is 22nd October 1992. Now, on the topic of Hadzici it states: "Ninety prisoners of war are accommodated in the Hadzici sports centre. Organisation and security is provided by the Hadzici Public Security Station." So firstly, you accept that this document contradicts your testimony that the Hadzici public security station was not involved in the organisation of the sports centre?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: In the organisation of the sports centre, I said at the very outset how it was. And after that a certain number of policemen together with members of the military provided security there. At first all members of the police were involved in repelling attacks at the front line. Once the situation was consolidated, at least a bit, then the police started doing their own work too. I think this has to do with a number of people who were not prisoners but rather victims of a failed exchange at the level of state commissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's speak about the exchange. Mr. Avlijas states that he suggested that people be transferred to a section of KPD Butmir but did not encounter understanding regarding the transfer because it depended on the exchange of prisoners of war of Serbian nationality held in the Tarcin Silos and in Pazaric. It's correct, isn't it, that people were held in the sports centre for the purposes of exchange?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: A large-scale exchange had been agreed upon at the level of state organs between the Muslim and Serb sides. On the Muslim side it was led by Mr. Amor Masevic [phoen]. All the people were asked about leaving Hadzici and also those who were in Pazarici and Tarcin who wanted to leave Muslim-controlled territory. How do I put this? People were polled. They were asked where they wanted to go and whether they wanted to be exchanged, and then they were told that on such and such a date an exchange would be carried out, buses were provided, and it was supposed to happen at the separation line between the municipalities of -- at the location called Kobiljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to the final paragraph in this section - and I believe it's the next page in the B/C/S - and it states: "In the cases of Zvornik, Hadzici, and Ilidza, we see that the Public Security Stations keep people in custody without any authorisation or justification in law because they have the authority to keep people in custody for no longer than three days." The people who are the subject of these -- of this document are not people who are part of any sort of organised exchange, are they? They are people who are being kept under illegal detention; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Really, I cannot answer. As far as I know, these were people who were prepared, I mean to have these exchanges take place from both sides. And there was a lot of pressure from families on our side and on the Muslim side and state commissions were working. However, these exchanges failed day after day and practically people stayed on for a long time without any need for them to stay on such premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's move to page 28 of the English of this document and page 27 of the B/C/S. And this is a letter of the same date from minister for justice Momcilo Mandic to the Serbian municipalities of Hadzici and Ilidza. And he states: "Having carried out the control of this ministry, we have established that there are 90 persons of Muslim ethnicity imprisoned on the territory of your municipality ..." Now -- sorry, "... on the territory of your municipality at the premises of the sports centre in Hadzici ..." Now, contrary to what you say at paragraph 9 of your statement, the sports centre wasn't a space for temporary accommodation, but these people were, in fact, imprisoned there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Temporary accommodation and prison in war time -- I mean, I don't know how I would make a distinction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that sentence, as the interpreters did not catch your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: The reception centre, if I can call it that, in war time at times when war is waged or this detention or these premises for keeping people, practically all of this boiled down to the same thing terminologically.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about some evidence before the Trial Chamber of one of the witnesses who was part of a failed exchange who testified - and this is Zihad Okic whose testimony is at -- evidence is at P124 and 125 - and Mr. Okic was under house arrest from the 11th of May until the 7th of September, 1992. And on the 7th of September, your colleague Zoran Gasevic came to his house and told him, his wife and his children, that they had half an hour to go to a meeting point where they would be bussed to an exchange at Kobiljaca. And Mr. Okic recounted that about 200 Muslims were picked up from around the villages and travelled to Kobiljaca where an exchange -- the anticipated exchange didn't, in fact, take place. And so they were then returned to the sports centre, around 500 people in total, where they were held, some of whom were held until - and this is Witness Misic's evidence - for 12 days; and that's P2403, paragraphs 113 to 117. Now, only on the 18th of September were the women and children released to go home, so that out of 500 detainees only 84 remained. So I'd just like to clarify what your evidence is on this. These witnesses -- these detainees were not, in fact, being voluntarily accommodated, were they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Well, just a moment ago I explained that a large-scale exchange had been agreed upon, all for all. And among other things, people were told: Pack, get on the buses, and we're going to Kobiljaca for an exchange. On the other side there will be buses too and numbers would not be looked at at all, how many people. So as many people on one side and as many people on the other side, but then what happened? On the Muslim side they obstructed this. They did not bring people. Their state commission went together with our state commission and they negotiated and they stayed until late at night and then Amor Masevic, the then-president of the state commission said that they did not want that but that talks would continue on the next day, and then on the next day these activities should continue in view of the fact that people had already packed their things, the bare necessities, things that they could take by bus. There was no point in taking them back to their homes. It was suggested - I don't know who it was from the state commission that suggested this - that they spend the night at the sports hall and that the buses would be prepared for the following day if this was ensured. However, how did this happen? Unfortunately, at Kobiljaca there was this -- actually all these buses actually left from both sides and Mr. Masevic and his driver and we took them to the police station in Hadzici and then he spent the night with -- at the house of the person who was then the chief and then he went on to Sarajevo to continue these activities and these activities because of the obstruction of the other side --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Tolj, once again I'll just ask you to keep your question -- your answers as concise as possible. My question is simply: Do you agree that people, including people who were being held for the purposes of exchange, were being held against their will at Hadzici sports centre?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I really cannot say that that was against their will. It was with their agreement because people had been told: You will wait here for the commissions to reach agreement and then we're going to have the exchanges effected. Now, the fact that this took some time and that practically this was undermined and this activity failed all together, so it turned out that these people were in captivity for longer than normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's speak then about some of the people who remained in captivity up until the 22nd of October which is the document that we've looked at. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from Mehmet Music, who was, for your information, one of the people who was taken to the garage -- municipality building garage from Musici and subsequently brought to the sports centre. So therefore, the police had determined that he was not a threat to them under your own account. And on the 23rd of October, Witness Music was transferred by the police, by the Hadzici police, together with 70 detainees to -- from the Hadzici sports centre to Planjo's house in Svrake, in Vogosca, and that's at P2403, paragraph 123. So this was a transfer that occurred during the period in which you were commander. Do you recall this transfer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Well, that was done on orders that arrived from the ministry to transfer. The first time when I spoke the capacities at the Kula prison were overextended. We did not know where the capacities were being extended and where else they could be kept. So the orders we received were for them to be transferred to Bajina Kula. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, in fact, individuals who your own police force had ascertained were no threat to you were transferred first to Kula prison, then to Lukavica, then back to Kula prison, back to the Hadzici sports centre and now to Planjo's house in Svrake. So, in fact, these civilians were not -- they didn't elect to be held at the sports centre; rather, they were transferred from detention centre to detention centre as the Hadzici authorities pleased. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Well, it's not that the police of Hadzici liked that or were pleased. The police in Hadzici didn't do that. There were exchanges that had been agreed upon. There were people who were brought for exchanges primarily. Also, there were private and individual ones, individual exchanges and exchanges at state levels, so some people were transferred from prison to Hadzici because these exchanges usually took place at Kobiljaca, at the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let me just clarify your evidence on this point. You say it's not that the police of Hadzici liked that or were pleased. And then the transcript reads: "The police in Hadzici didn't do that." Are you denying that the police in Hadzici were involved in moving detainees from detention centre to detention centre in Hadzici municipality and the surrounding municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: If they were given an assignment, then they would carry it out, that is to say they would effect the transfer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. McKenna. With the indulgence of the interpreters and reporter, we decided to go until 3.00, so if you could conclude by then, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolj, could you please give me answers that are as short as possible so that we can finish by 3.00. When did you leave Sarajevo and when did you get to Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Well, it was the beginning, April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the reason was for the fighting around the village of Musici?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Well, information was coming in to the effect that there was an armed group in Musici and that there was sporadic gun-fire from that area. This is a village with mixed population, Serb and Muslim. People felt unsafe, and an order was passed to cleanse the terrain and to collect the weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked, or rather, it was suggested that in the detention unit in the municipality only Muslims were being detained. Was anybody else being detained?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: There were Serbs too because in part these premises were used for police detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you said in line 89 -- on page 89 of today's transcript that it wasn't only the police that was detaining people who had violated the law, but also the army brought in those who were captured in fighting. Here it was said "combat" and "in combat zone" elsewhere. That is what was stated. Who was it the army brought into the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: The army brought in those who were taken prisoner during combat activities or if they found them with weapons, and so on, or if they intercepted various groups. There were things like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that as for civilians who had violated the law there was an obligation of three days of detention and then they would be brought before a judge. What about prisoners of war? Did they have to appear before an investigating judge within three days?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: It wasn't possible to organise that, to take them before an investigating judge because there wasn't an investigating judge in our area. We had not organised a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the whole, for prisoners of war was there this obligation to keep them in detention for up to three days and to bring them before an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you know this Mehmet Music and Adem Balic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I knew Adem Balic. As for Mehmet Music, I know he was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about people's departures and exchanges. Did any lists exist of people who were supposed to cross over to the Muslim side and how were those lists made?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Lists were made by going from person to person and asking them whether they wanted to cross over to have some sort of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who polled the Muslims in the Serbian territory of Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: In the Serb territory of Hadzici municipality, civilian commissioners existed by street, by neighbourhood, they dealt with distribution of food, and they also had lists of all inhabitants in their area, and they went from door to door and made those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Masovici and the Muslim side know how many Muslim civilians wanted to cross over?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, because they could see with their own eyes, they could talk with those people while they were waiting on buses, and it was evident that that was no forced deportation; that it was of their own free will that they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your experience, how long would a person's name be on the list before being informed that a bus would be available within one or two hours?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: That was very difficult because once we got information that something like that would be organised, that there would be a movement of population, that there is will on both sides, then we would approach people immediately, poll them, and based on that we made lists. So there were no precise time-frames.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 99 it was quoted to you that somebody came and told them: You have 30 minutes to get ready. Were you able to see that it was something forced or were they just given information when they would be able to leave?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Those people knew they would be leaving, they knew that in advance, and then they were told: The time has come. Get ready within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any Muslims who didn't put their names on those lists and stayed to live in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were Muslims like that but I don't know how many. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was some ambiguity here about the role of the Serb police in guarding the school centre. First of all, tell us, how far was the combat zone from Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: All of Hadzici was a combat zone. That belt was constantly shelled, shot at, perhaps there was a little part of Hadzici facing Ilidza close to the bridge that was a little spared from the shelling, but mainly shells would land almost every day on Hadzici except for brief periods of cease-fire if they were respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the number of casualties, how many were wounded and injured every day or at least in peak days of Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: In the early days four policemen were killed, five were wounded. In attacks on the 10th and 25th a large number of soldiers were killed, many were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Muslim soldiers take our soldiers prisoners and did our army keep Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were prisoners taken on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see D1074. It's a report by Mr. Glavas. This is related to transcript page 97. The question was: [In English] Do you accept that this document contradicts your testimony that the Hadzici public security station was not involved in the organisation of the sports centre? Your answer was: "In the organisation of the sports centre I said at the very outset how it was, and after that a certain number of policemen together with members of the military provided security there. At first, all members of the police were involved in repelling attacks at the front line. Once the situation was consolidated at least a bit then the police started doing their own work." [Interpretation] Could we now see the second page, please, in both versions. Item (b) says: "In the period April and July 1992 police officers of this station were involved in all combat operations and that was necessary at the time, indispensable, whereas beginning with 1 August 1992 most of the policemen had returned from the front lines and were again involved in the activities of the Ministry of the Interior. In April not a single policeman was involved in regular work and there were 105 in combat. In May, none in regular activities, 120 in combat. In June and July only 3 and 5 respectively were in regular activities. How is this consistent with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I too have confirmed that in the first two months policemen were non-stop on the front lines, and later on to the extent of our ability we got some of them to come back and do regular police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last document, on page 91 , lines 8 through 12, you were asked -- I'll read it in English: [In English] "Q. The detainees had no means of cleaning themselves, did they? "A. For hygiene they had the same facilities as everybody else." [Interpretation] Then you added: The police, army, and the population, none of that made it into the record. Did you mean police, army, and all the other population?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I meant everybody, the police, the army, and all the citizens. There was no water. The water was cut off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show 65 ter 24666. 65 ter 24666, page 3. Let's first see the cover page and then page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the work until December. Could you read the first three lines dealing with water-supply, or I can read it: "Water-supply. "After the war broke out there was a breakdown in water supply to the Serb municipality of Hadzici, so we were forced to make an improvised pipeline to re-route the well located at the Hadzici maintenance and repairs depot ..." et cetera. How does this fit with your knowledge about the availability of water?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: I could provide a broader explanation if there is time, but I know until 1994 there was no water in Hadzici. The local sources were reconnected using pumps and only closer parts of the town, wherever possible, received water, and the rest we provided through water tanks and distributed to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said there was no power, no electricity. Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is that your last question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm done with the documents. This is the last one. There will only be a brief question afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I read this to you: "As a result of war operations, electric power supply has been completely discontinued." How does that fit with your statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: It's true that the transmission line of 35 kilowatts was brought down and the breakdown was in such a place that we needed to secure the site first and we even tried through the UNPROFOR to provide joint works to repair it and that would last for a day or two and then it would break down again. So there were many days in Hadzici without water or electricity and there was just a little gas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 102 it was suggested to you in the question that those people who were taken from Hadzici to Kula then to Planjo's house were civilians. Did you consider those who were taken prisoner in combat or disarmed through some -- in some operations as civilians?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN TOLJ
utterances.text: Of course they were not civilians. They were captured in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have completed my examination. May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3064, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you have any comment on the Defence motion for modification of segregation regime for certain witness, you will be heard first thing on Monday. Mr. Tolj, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go. We'll rise all together and resume --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may, if I may ask whether Prosecution was segregated from their own witnesses during their own case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's not on the list of next week's witnesses list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he won't be testifying next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
